title: The People Who Left Kangaroo Island
place: Lashmars Lagoon, Dudley Peninsula, Kangaroo Island, South Australia, Australia
text: A seven-metre sediment core from Lashmars Lagoon on Kangaroo Island's Dudley Peninsula helped Adelaide University researchers show that the last reliable evidence of people on the island is at least about 5,000 years old, in line with Indigenous oral histories of people leaving. Afterwards fire stayed rare for another 3,000 years in a wetter climate, then increased over the past 2,000 years as it dried.

source.name: Adelaide University News (2026): Ancient sediments on Kangaroo Island show climate change drove fire activity in the absence of people

title: A 5,000-Year-Old Island Midden
place: Maizie Bay, Konomie (North Keppel Island), Queensland, Australia
text: On Konomie (North Keppel Island), off central Queensland, archaeologist Mike Rowland excavated and radiocarbon dated a midden at Maizie Bay to nearly 5,000 years old. The Woppaburra describe their ancestors as sea-faring saltwater people, island specialists who travelled between Konomie, Woppa (Great Keppel) and other islands for seasonal food. Konomie is their spiritual motherland and creation place.

source.name: Australian Museum: Woppaburra people of the Keppel Islands (Woppaburra Land Trust)

title: The Fire-Devil From the Sun
place: Henbury Meteorites Conservation Reserve, Northern Territory, Australia
text: Around 4,700 years ago a large nickel-iron meteoroid blazed across the Central Australian sky, and its fragments carved out more than a dozen craters up to 180 metres across. Luritja elders later said this was where a fire-devil ran down from the sun, set the land ablaze and killed people. Rainwater pooling in the craters was forbidden, for fear the fire-devil would fill drinkers with iron.

source.name: UNSW Newsroom (Duane Hamacher): Finding meteorite impacts in Aboriginal oral tradition

title: Stone Axes on the Move
place: Sydney region, New South Wales, Australia
text: About 4,500 years ago ground-edged stone axes appeared in south-eastern Australia. Usually made from tough igneous or metamorphic rock, they were traded across nations along routes often up to 200 km long, and one axe head in the Australian Museum travelled 1,000 km from its source. Gadigal people in Sydney called them mogo and used them to make bark canoes, cut wood, hunt and build shelters.

source.name: Australian Museum: First Nations timeline

title: The Stranded People of Flinders Island
place: Flinders Island, Furneaux Group, Tasmania, Australia
text: Rising seas flooded the land bridge to Tasmania and left a group of people on Flinders Island in Bass Strait. Radiocarbon-dated middens show people lived there until about 4,500 years ago, then disappeared. Archaeologist Robin Sim found no sign that they had watercraft, so the middens were probably left by an isolated, stranded population, whose decline he linked to a mid-Holocene climate shift.

source.name: ANU Open Research: Robin Sim, The archaeology of isolation? Prehistoric occupation in the Furneaux Group of Islands (PhD thesis, 1998)

title: When the Bullin Shrieked
place: Mount Gambier, South Australia, Australia
text: The most recent volcanic activity at Mount Gambier and Mount Schank happened about 4,300 years ago. An Aboriginal story tells of Craitbul and his family, who buried food overnight to cook in earth ovens on Mount Muirhead until the bullin shrieked in the night. They fled to Mount Schank, then Mount Gambier, where their ovens flooded. Researcher Patrick Nunn sees an ancient memory of eruptions.

source.name: The Conversation (Patrick D. Nunn): When the bullin shrieked: Aboriginal memories of volcanic eruptions thousands of years ago

title: Return to Vanderlin Island
place: Vanderlin Island, Sir Edward Pellew Group, Northern Territory, Australia
text: Rising seas cut Vanderlin Island, in the Gulf of Carpentaria, off from the mainland about 6,700 years ago, and people seem to have moved to higher ground. Archaeologists Robin Sim and Lynley Wallis found a gap of several thousand years in its record, then signs that people steadily recolonised these new islands from about 4,200 years ago, with occupation growing after 1,300 years ago.

source.name: Australian Archaeology 67 (2008), Sim and Wallis: Northern Australian offshore island use during the Holocene: the archaeology of Vanderlin Island (ANU Research Portal)

title: Clay-Ball Ovens of the Murray
place: Calperum Station, Riverland, South Australia, Australia
text: On the Murray River floodplain at Calperum Station, Aboriginal people built earth-oven mounds from at least about 4,000 years ago and used them until European invasion. Flinders University researchers and the River Murray and Mallee Aboriginal Corporation excavated six mounds and found charcoal, mussel shell and clay balls that held heat in underground ovens, probably used to cook bulrush tubers for food and fibre.

source.name: ANSTO: Murray River earth mounds reveal Aboriginal cooking practices spanning 4000 years

source2.name: Flinders University Research: Aboriginal earth mounds of the Calperum floodplain (The Holocene, 2022)

dateLabel: Before about 1300 BCE (at least 3,300 years ago)
title: Tasselled Figures Under a Wasp Nest
place: Lawley River area, northwest Kimberley, Western Australia, Australia
text: In the northwest Kimberley, Mambi Gwion figures, also called Tassel Bradshaws, are painted in red with a darker red outline, tassels on the head, clearly drawn fingers and a paunch. A mud wasp nest over a 'cage-shape' motif painted on top of them gave a minimum age of about 3,300 years, which indirectly dates the figures underneath to earlier still.

source.name: PLOS ONE (2016), Ross, Westaway, Travers, Morwood and Hayward: Into the Past: A Step Towards a Robust Kimberley Rock Art Chronology (PMC)

title: Torres Strait's First Gardens
place: Dauar, Murray Islands, Torres Strait, Queensland, Australia
text: On Dauar, one of the Murray Islands in eastern Torres Strait, excavations in 1998 to 2000 revealed widespread land clearance and gardening from at least 2,000 years ago, the earliest horticulture yet established in the strait. Plant traces such as starch grains supported this. Sand in Dauar's pottery, dated 2,000 to 700 years ago, points to New Guinea and exchange with Papuan lowland groups.

source.name: JCU ResearchOnline: M. J. Carter, North of the Cape and south of the Fly: the archaeology of settlement and subsistence on the Murray Islands (PhD thesis, 2004)

title: Coming Back to Dabangay
place: Dabangay, Mabuyag, Torres Strait, Queensland, Australia
text: Dabangay, on the island of Mabuyag in western Torres Strait, is one of only two known mid-Holocene sites in the strait. Eleven new radiocarbon dates, combined with nine earlier ones, show people lived there for a long stretch from about 7,200 to 3,200 years ago, then barely used it. Around 1,815 years ago a second sustained settlement began, and it has lasted right up to the present.

source.name: Australian Archaeology 76 (2013), Wright: short report on the re-excavation of Dabangay, Mabuyag (Australian Archaeological Association)

title: Older Than the Linguists Thought
place: Nalkurdalayarrb, Sweers Island, South Wellesley Islands, Queensland, Australia
text: The South Wellesley Islands in the Gulf of Carpentaria are Kaiadilt country, and reaching Bentinck Island from the mainland needs a 10 km open-water crossing. Linguists had suggested people first arrived within the last 1,000 years. But a radiocarbon date from a shell midden at Nalkurdalayarrb on Sweers Island shows occupation by about 1,580 years ago, almost double that estimate.

source.name: Australian Archaeology (2010), Ulm et al.: Radiocarbon and linguistic dates for occupation of the South Wellesley Islands (JCU ResearchOnline)

title: Island-Made Pots on Mabuyag
place: Mui, Mabuyag, Torres Strait, Queensland, Australia
text: In 2006 archaeologists digging a one-metre square at Mui, on Mabuyag in western Torres Strait, found two joining pottery sherds 1.35 metres down. Charcoal above and below dated them to about 1,300 to 1,600 years ago. The sand in the clay came from Mabuyag itself, so these thin-walled plain pots were made locally, perhaps after pottery technology reached the region about 1,700 years ago.

source.name: Australian Archaeology (2009), Wright and Dickinson: Movement of ideas not materials: locally manufactured pottery on Mabuyag Island (ANU Open Research)

title: The Vanishing Bondi Points
place: Bondi, Sydney, New South Wales, Australia
text: Small stone tools called backed artefacts, or microliths, appeared in Sydney's archaeological record and then disappeared about 1,500 years ago. Once nicknamed Bondi points after the suburb where they were first identified, they have one blunted side, perhaps for gripping or fixing to a spear shaft or gum handle. Microscope and residue studies suggest uses from woodworking and skin-working to spear points and scarification.

source.name: Australian Museum: First Nations timeline

title: Spirits Painted on Dauan
place: Kabadul Kula, Dauan, Torres Strait, Queensland, Australia
text: Kabadul Kula, a painted boulder shelter on Dauan island just 10 km from the Papua New Guinea coast, holds 47 red ochre paintings, among them a dogai female spirit, dancing figures, a crayfish and canoes. Digging beneath one panel, archaeologists found ochre fragments, most dropped between 1,200 and 1,400 years ago, linked to an early phase of painting. They were then Torres Strait's oldest rock art dates.

source.name: Australian Archaeology 69 (2009): Kabadul Kula and the Antiquity of Torres Strait Rock Art (ANU Open Research)

title: Boulders Tended for Centuries
place: Packsaddle Valley, Pilbara, Western Australia, Australia
text: Near Packsaddle Valley in the Pilbara, people built a stone arrangement complex at least 1,360 years ago. Luminescence dating of sediment trapped beneath the boulders shows they returned to re-erect fallen stones at least twice, about 800 and 480 years ago. Care for the site seems to have ended around 380 years ago, when four boulders toppled over.

source.name: Journal of Archaeological Science: Reports 49 (2023), Gliganic, Slack and Meyer: Tending to tradition: Dating stone arrangement maintenance in northwest Australia (JCU ResearchOnline)

title: A Busy Southeast Queensland Coast
place: Moreton Bay, Queensland, Australia
text: Radiocarbon dates from Aboriginal sites across southeast Queensland tell a striking story. Archaeologists Sean Ulm and Jay Hall found that big increases in the number of occupied sites, and in how quickly new sites were set up, came only after about 1,200 years ago, and only along the coastal strip. They argued this was a real change in how people lived, not just a quirk of preservation.

source.name: Australian Archaeology '95 (Tempus 6, 1996), Ulm and Hall: Radiocarbon and cultural chronologies in southeast Queensland prehistory (JCU ResearchOnline)

title: Where the Old People Lived
place: Wirrngaji, Bentinck Island, South Wellesley Islands, Queensland, Australia
text: Kaiadilt elder Dawn Naranatjil pointed out Wirrngaji, a large shell midden on an old beach ridge on Bentinck Island, as a promising place to dig, 'where the old people used to live'. A small test pit found a thin lower shell layer dated to about 1,048 years ago, beneath a thick upper layer about 860 years old. Glass on the surface shows people lived there into recent times.

source.name: Australian Archaeology (2010), Ulm et al.: Radiocarbon and linguistic dates for occupation of the South Wellesley Islands (JCU ResearchOnline)

title: Dugong Feasts at Goemu Village
place: Goemu village, Mabuyag, Torres Strait, Queensland, Australia
text: Goemu village on Mabuyag has one of the largest midden deposits recorded in Torres Strait. One of its long mounded middens formed about 950 to 1,000 years ago, from a way of life centred on hunting dugong and turtle, topped up with fishing and shellfishing on nearby reef flats and mangroves. Land snails show that shade trees once grew where grassland is now.

source.name: Memoirs of the Queensland Museum, Cultural Heritage Series (2015), McNiven et al.: Midden formation and marine specialisation at Goemu village, Mabuyag (Monash University)

title: Mountains of Shell at Weipa
place: Mandjungaar, Weipa Peninsula, Cape York, Queensland, Australia
text: More than 500 shell mounds dot the Weipa area of western Cape York Peninsula. At Mandjungaar, at the request of Ndrua'angayth custodians, archaeologists dated a dome-shaped mound and found people began building it about 800 years ago, adding to it for centuries. Most shells came from one bivalve, Tegillarca granosa, from intertidal mudflats. A neighbouring mound stands 4 metres high.

source.name: Queensland Archaeological Research 21 (2018), Morrison, Wight and Evans: Report on excavation of a shell mound site at Mandjungaar

dateLabel: Before about 1360 CE (at least 650 years ago)
title: A Star-Yam on the Shelter Wall
place: Upper Bush Spirit Creek, northwest Kimberley, Western Australia, Australia
text: At the headwaters of Bush Spirit Creek in the northwest Kimberley, a large motif painted in a 'star-yam' form covers the back wall of a big rockshelter. Mud wasps later built a nest over it, and luminescence dating of the nest gave a minimum age of about 650 years. The method reads a light-sensitive signal that builds up while grains stay covered.

source.name: PLOS ONE (2016), Ross, Westaway, Travers, Morwood and Hayward: Into the Past: A Step Towards a Robust Kimberley Rock Art Chronology (PMC)
